title: France consumer confidence plunges to lowest since 2013 as fiscal worries deepen
summary: France October consumer confidence 80 vs 85 expected Prior 86; revised to 85 That's a major blow. French household confidence falls to its lowest since 2013 in October as fiscal worries and concerns over the country's public finances weigh heavily on sentiment. That is not a good look as the index strays further away from the long-term average of 100, in which we haven't seen since December 2021. There were marked deteriorations in sentiment among most sub-indices, as households noted worsening past and expected financial situations. Meanwhile, the sub-index measuring past and future standard of living conditions also showed a big drop in October. Adding to those concerns, consumers are also fearing that inflation pressures are going to worsen in the months ahead. The sub-index measuring futures prices rose further to -7 points, its highest since May, and is well off the -32 points recorded in July. Besides that, unemployment fears also picked up with the sub-index there rising by another 5 points to 61 points on the month. That marks the highest level since March 2021. It's an all-round poor report as it signals that the French consumer climate has deterioriated markedly amid the social unrest and fiscal woes. And we're already starting to see that show up in economic data too, with French PMI figures this month already being rather disappointing. summary: EUROPEAN SESSION In the European session, we don't have much on the agenda other than a couple of low-tier releases like the French consumer confidence and the Spanish unemployment rate. AMERICAN SESSION In the American session, we get the US durable goods orders and the US consumer confidence report. Again, the data won't change anything for the Fed, so the market reaction will likely be muted. The focus remains on the Middle East as oil prices continue to make multi-month highs, weighing further on growth and inflation concerns. We have also the Israeli elections today but I'm not sure how a change of leadership would alter the current picture. Many opposition figures support maintaining pressure on Iran. The one having a drastically different view is opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot said he believes economic pressure is the best way to defeat Iran.
